chapters.title: A Letter That Changed Its Mind
chapters.teaser: Jude says he had to abandon a warmer letter to write this urgent one instead.
body: "When I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith" (v.3). Jude confesses he planned a different letter — something about shared salvation, presumably encouraging — but events forced his hand toward something sharper and more urgent.

The faith he calls readers to defend was "once delivered unto the saints" — a fixed, received deposit, not something each generation invents fresh. That phrase sets up the whole letter's stakes: this isn't a difference of opinion to be debated politely, but a settled inheritance under active attack from people who had "crept in unawares" among the community (v.4).

chapters.title: Three Warnings from Israel's Past
chapters.teaser: Jude reaches for three ancient precedents to show that privilege doesn't prevent judgment.
body: In rapid succession, Jude cites the wilderness generation whom the Lord "saved... out of the land of Egypt" yet "afterward destroyed... that believed not" (v.5), angels who "kept not their first estate" and are held "in everlasting chains under darkness" (v.6), and Sodom and Gomorrah, "suffering the vengeance of eternal fire" (v.7) as a public example.

The common thread across all three is that each group started with real standing — rescued Israelites, heavenly angels, cities under God's provision — and still fell under judgment through rebellion. Jude is arguing from a pattern: being inside the community, even inside heaven itself, has never been a guarantee against consequences for those who abandon their calling.

chapters.title: Even an Archangel Held His Tongue
chapters.teaser: Michael's restraint toward the devil exposes just how reckless the false teachers really are.
body: In a striking, non-biblical tradition (echoing the Jewish text known as the Assumption of Moses), Jude recalls that "Michael the archangel, when contending with the devil he disputed about the body of Moses, durst not bring against him a railing accusation, but said, The Lord rebuke thee" (v.9). Even Michael, facing Satan directly, refused to hurl personal insults and instead deferred the verdict to God.

That restraint becomes the standard against which the false teachers are measured and found reckless: "these speak evil of those things which they know not" (v.10), slandering realities far above their own authority while indulging, "as brute beasts," whatever their bodies want. If an archangel wouldn't presume to judge Satan with his own words, Jude implies, these teachers have wildly overstepped their place.

chapters.title: Waterless Clouds and Wandering Stars
chapters.teaser: Jude piles up nature images to expose false teachers as all promise and no substance.
body: Verses 12-13 read almost like a poem of accusation: "spots in your feasts of charity... clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots; raging waves of the sea, foaming out their own shame; wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever."

Each image targets the same failure from a different angle — clouds that promise rain and deliver none, trees that should bear fruit but are doubly dead, stars that should hold a fixed course but wander into darkness. These are people who look impressive and confident inside the community's own shared meals, but produce nothing real, and the very nature imagery meant to evoke stability instead exposes their instability.

chapters.title: Enoch's Prophecy and a Doxology
chapters.teaser: Jude quotes a text outside the Bible, then ends with one of Scripture's most quoted blessings.
body: Jude directly quotes 1 Enoch, a Jewish apocalyptic writing outside the Hebrew canon, attributing to "Enoch also, the seventh from Adam" a prophecy of the Lord coming "with ten thousands of his saints, to execute judgment upon all" (v.14-15). It's a rare moment where a New Testament writer openly cites material beyond the Old Testament, showing Jude's readers were fluent in a wider body of Jewish apocalyptic tradition, not just Torah and Prophets.

After all the warning, the letter pivots to instruction and hope: believers are to keep "building up yourselves on your most holy faith," praying in the Spirit, and keeping themselves "in the love of God" while showing mercy to the wavering and pulling others "out of the fire" (v.20-23). It closes with the doxology many churches still recite: praise to the God "that is able to keep you from falling, and to present you faultless... with exceeding joy" (v.24) — assurance that outlasts every warning that came before it.
